oil.summary: Crude gave back a chunk of last week's geopolitical risk premium on Wednesday, with WTI falling 3.61% to $101.99 and Brent dropping 2.96% to $105.53, though both contracts remain up sharply on the month. The sell-off looks corrective rather than structural: the underlying supply picture stays deeply stressed. Iran's blockade of Hormuz persists — Tehran vowing it continues until attacks end — while Russia extended its diesel export ban through October 31, citing refinery delays. Mutual Russia-Ukraine strikes on oil infrastructure add further complexity. Tanker rates breaching $1 million per day for the first time on record underscore physical market tightness. Downstream, RBOB gasoline cratered 6.71% and heating oil shed 5.34%, suggesting some demand-side softening after the EIA reported a modest 600,000-barrel draw in U.S. crude inventories. The U.S. House advancing a Russia sanctions bill that could hit India with 100% tariffs on Russian oil purchases adds a significant wild card to trade-flow assumptions.
drivers: Strait of Hormuz crisis: Iranian vessel struck, Iran blockade ongoing, Houthi expansion threatening tanker routes — spot freight rates hit record $1 million/day
Russia diesel export ban extended to October 31 and mutual Russia-Ukraine strikes on oil infrastructure keep medium-distillate markets tight despite today's price pullback
Soft U.S. demand signal: EIA crude draw only 600k bbl while RBOB -6.71% on the day suggests gasoline demand is easing, capping the upside despite geopolitical tension

gas.summary: European TTF shed 3.10% to €77.58/MWh on the day, though the month-on-month print of +25.62% tells the real story — markets remain historically elevated and close to 2022 highs, per headlines noting TTF touched €80+ intraday. Low European storage volumes are sustaining the structural bid. Qatar exports staying blocked is driving buyers toward alternatives: Equinor announced plans to scale its LNG portfolio to 10–15 million tons annually by the early 2030s to fill that gap. Southeast Asian LNG demand is also surging, driven by AI data-center load growth, though the headline flags concern that prolonged price spikes could curb the very investment needed to meet it. Saudi pipeline attacks on September 10 are beginning to ripple into European energy markets, adding an oil-to-gas substitution risk premium. Henry Hub, by contrast, was nearly flat at $2.893/MMBtu (-0.89%), reflecting continued domestic U.S. supply-demand balance.
drivers: European storage deficits and Qatar export blockade keeping TTF structurally elevated near €80/MWh despite today's pullback; Equinor accelerating LNG expansion to 15 Mt/yr to compensate
Saudi East-West Pipeline attacks on September 10 are feeding into European energy risk premia as Saudi oil supply disruption threatens gas-to-power substitution dynamics
AI-driven LNG demand surge in Southeast Asia tightening the global LNG balance and competing with European buyers for scarce cargoes

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs fell 3.17% to $81.14/EUA today, tracking a broad energy complex sell-off alongside TTF's 3.10% decline. The month-on-month gain of +4.27% on EUAs remains modest relative to TTF's +25.62% surge, suggesting the carbon market has not fully priced the fuel-switching implications of persistently high gas. A leaked EU Commission document on RED IV signals a potential shift away from specific hydrogen mandates toward an EU-wide target, which, if confirmed, could reduce compliance demand from electrolyser operators and weigh on near-term carbon co-benefits. Geopolitical headlines — the Hormuz crisis, Russia sanctions, and the U.S. advancing secondary tariff legislation targeting Indian purchases of Russian oil — are the dominant macro frame for European power, as gas import risk remains acute. Today's headline noting WTI above $100 pushing U.S. fuel prices to new records underlines the broader inflationary energy backdrop European power buyers face heading into the winter.
drivers: EUA prices down 3.17% in sympathy with TTF selloff, yet month-on-month carbon underperformance vs. gas suggests market is not fully pricing fuel-switching demand into EUAs
Leaked RED IV draft proposing to scrap specific hydrogen mandates in favour of an EU-wide target is a structural bearish signal for hydrogen-linked carbon demand
Ongoing Hormuz disruption and Saudi pipeline damage sustain a high-gas-cost / supply-insecurity backdrop that could force increased coal burn in European power, raising EUA demand this winter
